title: Discovering Differences in Strategic Behavior between Humans and LLMs
claim: A baseline behavioral model uses simple value learning; the discovered model adds richer opponent modeling and counterfactual value updates.
layout: 2 panels split by dotted line, flow top-to-bottom, colored module boxes with arrows
description: Two large computation-graph diagrams are separated by a vertical dotted line. The left diagram shows the discovered human program. The right one shows the more elaborate Gemini 2.5 Pro program. Inputs sit at the top as small hatched colored squares: opponent choice in red, own choice in green, reward in blue. Arrows carry them down through boxes and circled minus and plus operators. A pink shaded region labeled opponent modeling and a light-blue shaded region labeled value learning group the modules. A blue 3D cube stands for the Q-value array. The outputs are choice logits at the bottom. The right panel is visibly more complex. It adds a transition matrix, counterfactual rewards and prediction errors, and several update steps. A small legend at the bottom center explains input, output and agent-state textures.
caption: Diagrams of AlphaEvolve-discovered programs. The simplest-but-best programs for humans (left) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (right), discovered by AlphaEvolve on iterated rock-paper-scissors, are displayed. For simplicity, the learnable parameters θ of each program are omitted. Both programs use value-based learning and opponent modeling. The Gemini 2.5 Pro program displays more sophisticated opponent modeling than humans and considers counterfactual outcomes during value updates.
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in social and strategic scenarios, it becomes critical to understand where and why their behavior diverges from that of humans. While behavioral game theory (BGT) provides a framework for analyzing behavior, existing models do not fully capture the idiosyncratic behavior of humans or black-box, non-human agents like LLMs. We employ AlphaEvolve, a cutting-edge program discovery tool, to directly discover interpretable models of human and LLM behavior from data, thereby enabling open-ended discovery of structural factors driving human and LLM behavior. Our analysis on iterated rock-paper-scissors reveals that frontier LLMs can be capable of deeper strategic behavior than humans. These results provide a foundation for understanding structural differences driving differences in human and LLM behavior in strategic interactions.
